paper_title: EvalResearchBench: Can AI Agents Build Their Own Feedback for Recursive Self-Improvement?

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) relies on evaluation feedback to assess progress and guide further research, yet repeatedly running complex benchmarks is costly and slows iteration. Human experts reduce this cost by selecting benchmark subsets or designing compact suites. We ask whether AI agents can automate this design process and introduce EvalResearchBench (ERB), a benchmark for autonomous evaluation research. Given target materials, development references, candidate APIs, and fixed time and API budgets, an agent called the researcher selects or synthesizes tasks, implements graders, and revises them in pilot tests before freezing an executable evaluator for coding, co-work, and reasoning. We study 9 researchers and 13 candidate models and compare each frozen evaluator with 14 target benchmarks on score concordance and pairwise agreement. The best evaluators order about 75\% of candidate pairs as the targets do, below the 91\% ceiling set by disagreements among the targets. No researcher leads on every metric, and the best evaluator on development targets is not the best on sealed targets hidden from the researcher. A human-designed sample of public tasks remains a strong baseline, and the evaluator with the lowest recorded execution cost attains the highest pairwise agreement. Agents repair tasks and graders through pilot feedback, yet their evaluators can still truncate answers, exhaust the evaluation budget, or let a few questions dominate a domain score.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) relies on evaluation feedback to determine whether change improves system and which direction to explore next. Each new training recipe, dataset, or program creates another version to assess. Repeatedly running complex benchmarks incurs API and compute costs and delays the next experiment, particularly when evaluation requires long tool-using trajectories or specialized environments. Human experts reduce this burden by selecting representative subsets or designing cheaper proxies, as in tinyBenchmarks (Maia Polo et al., 2024). An autonomous improvement loop would need to perform this design step itself and obtain feedback that is informative enough to guide decisions and cheap enough to repeat. Recent work automates improvement while relying on supplied evaluation protocols. In PostTrainBench, agents choose data and post-training algorithms, but the target benchmark and evaluation harness are fixed (Rank et al., 2026). RSIBench-Data lets agents revise training-data strategies using checkpoint scores and trajectories from fixed evaluation service (Meng et al., 2026). AlphaEvolve evolves programs using user-provided evaluation function, with optional user-specified test cascades to screen proposals efficiently (Novikov et al., 2025). In each case, humans decide what to test, how to score it, and how to keep repeated measurement affordable, so extending autonomy to new domain still requires human-designed evaluation. Other work automates parts of evaluation design. PACE selects inexpensive source questions and calibrates them against expensive agentic targets (Song et al., 2026). AutoBencher and BenchAgents automate benchmark construction and refinement (Li et al., 2025; Butt et al., 2025), and BenchBench compares the quality of model-designed suites (Zheng et al., 2026). None of these settings poses the full research problem, in which an agent chooses measurement strategy, spends limited experimental budget, and revises an executable evaluator until it tracks complex target benchmarks. Solving it requires inspecting target evidence, choosing or creating tasks, verifying graders, and deciding whether pilot failure calls for harder questions, different coverage, repaired rubric, or more execution budget. We therefore ask whether an agent with fixed time and API budgets can build an evaluator that reproduces how complex target benchmarks score and rank models. We call this capability autonomous evaluation research. To address these gaps, we introduce EvalResearchBench (ERB), in which the researcher designs the measurement itself, pays for every pilot from fixed budget, and submits an executable evaluator that is scored against complex target benchmarks. researcher is model in an agent harness that designs the evaluator, candidate is model being tested, and target benchmark is an established evaluation whose candidate scores the evaluator should reproduce. The researcher receives target descriptions, permitted tasks and grading resources, execution traces, development reference scores, and APIs for development candidates (Figure 2). In pilot tests, it observes candidate responses, costs, and agreement with the visible references, then revises its tasks, graders, weights, and answer allowances. It then freezes an evaluator that returns one score per domain. Sealed candidates and targets stay hidden during research, so the researcher can neither call those candidates nor see those reference scores. Independent assessment runs the frozen evaluator on all candidates under separate budget and compares its scores with both development and sealed targets. We evaluate 9 researcher configurations, each model in the Codex or Claude Code harness run for one episode, on 13 open-weight and proprietary candidates and 14 target benchmarks in coding, co-work, and reasoning  (Table 1)  . These domains cover the implementation, professional work, and analysis that autonomous research relies on. As baseline, Random120 samples public tasks under fixed source quotas designed by humans. We measure agreement in two ways. Score is 100 times Lins concordance correlation coefficient between measured and reference scores (Lin, 1989), so it rewards matching score level and spread as well as order. Pairwise agreement (PA) is the fraction of candidate pairs that the evaluator orders as the target does. We also separate the one-time cost of building an evaluator from the cost of running it, which recurs for every new candidate. No evaluator leads in every domain (Figure 1). Grok 4.7 leads coding, Astra leads co-work, and Opus 5 leads reasoning, while coding is the weakest domain for most evaluators. Astra attains the highest overall Score and Grok 4.7 the highest PA. Even the best PA, about 75%, stays well below the 91% ceiling set by disagreements among the targets. Fable 5.1 has the highest Score on development

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: 2.1 EVALUATION DESIGN AND EFFICIENT MEASUREMENT Evaluation design spans coverage and standardization (Ribeiro et al., 2020; Liang et al., 2023; Kiela et al., 2021), task construction (Perez et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023a; Xia et al., 2024), and automated grading (Liu et al., 2023c; Zheng et al., 2023). AutoBencher refines datasets using model feedback (Li et al., 2025); BenchAgents integrates planning, generation, verification, and evaluation (Butt et al., 2025); BenchBench assesses benchmark designers through validity, discrimination, and ranking reliability (Zheng et al., 2026). Efficient measurement offers another route: APTBench transforms agent tasks and trajectories into lightweight questions (Qin et al., 2025), while tinyBenchmarks, Fluid Benchmarking, and Efficient Benchmarking of AI Agents study selection, estimation, and adaptive testing (Maia Polo et al., 2024; Hofmann et al., 2025; Ndzomga, 2026). Agent Psychometrics models task-level performance from task and system features (Ge et al., 2026). ERB evaluates an agents ability to choose and develop measurement strategies through autonomous, budgeted experimentation. 2.2 AUTONOMOUS RESEARCH AND SELF-IMPROVEMENT Research benchmarks study iterative experimentation (Huang et al., 2024; Nathani et al., 2025), resource-bounded machine-learning research (Chan et al., 2025; Wijk et al., 2025), replication (Starace et al., 2025), and post-training (Rank et al., 2026). The AI Scientist and Agent Laboratory integrate multiple stages of scientific work (Lu et al., 2024; Schmidgall et al., 2025). Self-improvement systems such as FunSearch, AlphaEvolve, and the Darwin Gödel Machine use evaluation feedback to guide program or agent revisions (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024; Novikov et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026); MIRROR and TRIAGE study self-knowledge and resource alloca-

sections.title: 3.1 RESEARCH TASK
sections.content: Researcher, candidates, and targets. The researcher is an LLM agent equipped with harness that lets it inspect files, write and execute code, call models, and revise its work. candidate is modelexecution configuration whose capabilities the researcher must measure. target benchmark provides the reference candidate scores that the resulting evaluation should reproduce. We cover three complementary capabilities needed for autonomous research. Coding supports implementing and testing systems, from repository engineering to scientific programming and terminal workflows (Huang et al., 2026; Tian et al., 2024a; Merrill et al., 2026). Co-work covers gathering information, following constraints, and producing professional deliverables (He et al., 2025; Wei et al., 2025; Patwardhan et al., 2025). Reasoning covers analytical work with academic questions, long documents, and specialized physics (Phan et al., 2025; Artificial Analysis, 2025a; Zhu et al., 2025). single research episode designs an evaluation across all three domains, allowing the agent to share resources and choose where further testing is most useful. Input materials. We provide target descriptions, available original tasks and grading resources, historical execution traces, and reference scores for development candidates. The researcher also receives metered candidate-model APIs, an execution SDK, and the submission contract. Resource availability varies by target; the agent may select existing tasks, synthesize new ones, or combine both approaches. Development tests return candidate responses and grading results for diagnosing errors and improving correlation with the visible target references. Budgets. We constrain three costs: researcher inference pays for the agents analysis and tool use; development testing pays for candidate and helper-model calls; independent assessment pays to execute the frozen design. Keeping the first two budgets separate prevents agent deliberation from consuming the testing allowance. fixed deadline limits research time. Section 4.1 gives the numerical limits. The researcher may select, synthesize, or simplify tasks, repair graders, change task weights, set answer allowances, and inspect pilot responses. Calls and retries pass through metered gateway. The agent allocates its development budget across exploration, testing, and revision without prescribed sequence. Submission. To require reusable test suite rather than few demonstrations, the agent submits at least 100 distinct scored questions, together with executable graders and fixed aggregation rules. The program returns one measured score per domain from candidate responses and frozen assets, without candidate-identity lookup or access to reference labels during scoring. Questions, grading code, and weights are frozen before assessment. One ERB entry is one research episode by particular model and harness. 3.2 INDEPENDENT ASSESSMENT To test transfer beyond development feedback, we execute the frozen program independently on development and withheld candidates and compare its scores with visible and withheld target references. Candidate access and target-reference access are assigned separately  (Table 1)  . The executor records per-item rewards, termination reasons, and usage. total assessment cap limits the cost of evaluating the candidate panel, while per-candidate cap bounds the cost of applying the design to any one model. Assessment is charged separately from development, and its results are not returned to the researcher for further revision. graded response is complete under the submitted contract, including wrong or empty answer at the output cap. sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: 4.1 SETUP We compare how different LLM researchers use the available materials and budget to build evaluations. The experiments first assess the resulting measurements, then examine the design choices and costs behind them. Appendix traces how these choices arise during research. Models. We study nine researcher configurations: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI, 2026c), GPT-5.6 Sol (OpenAI, 2026b), GLM-5.3 (Z.ai, 2026b), DeepSeek V4 Pro (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2026), Kimi K3 (Kimi Team et al., 2026), Fable 5.1 (Anthropic, 2026b), Opus 5 (Anthropic, 2026c), Grok 4.7 (xAI, 2026), and Fable 5 (Anthropic, 2026a). Each contributes one research episode. The GPT researchers and Grok use Codex (OpenAI, 2025a); the other researchers use Claude Code (Anthropic, 2025). The candidate panel contains four development-visible and nine sealed models  (Table 1)  . Budgets and implementation. The research budget is three hours, $100 for researcher inference, and $100 for shared development/helper testing. Independent assessment has $120 total cap and $30 per-candidate cap. Pilots may use smaller suites than the final submission; the researcher allocates its development calls freely.

sections.content: Overall results and domain strengths. Astra leads overall Score, whereas Grok leads PA: reproducing score levels and recovering candidate order favor different designs. Domain strengths also vary, with no researcher dominating both metrics across all three domains. Decomposing CCC as rCb helps explain why: Astra and GLM-5.3 have similar co-work correlations, but Astra aligns more closely with the reference scale  (Table 10)  . useful ordering alone does not guarantee faithful score reproduction. Development and sealed targets reveal different strengths. Fable 5.1 leads development Score, but Grok leads sealed Score. This reversal makes cross-target transfer distinct requirement for evaluation research: useful design must preserve capability signals beyond the references used to develop it. Systematic score shifts across targets within the same domain (Figure 7) further show why strong fit to one benchmark does not establish broadly useful evaluator. Public-task sampling is strong baseline. Random120s public sources, domain quotas, and graders encode task-design knowledge, making it strong baseline, especially in coding. Its coding and reasoning coverage recovers much of the candidate ordering, while Astras Score gains concentrate in co-work and reasoning (Figure 3). DeepSeek V4 Pro illustrates why iteration alone need not beat this baseline. It revises coding tasks and increases reasoning allowances, yet its short, deterministic coding and co-work checks yield scores clustered near the ceiling; its reasoning gains cannot offset the coding deficit. Research adds value when it identifies tasks that preserve target-relevant differences between candidates. Ease of grading and repeated revision do not by themselves ensure informative measurements. We analyze three design decisionstask selection, question count, and aggregationby varying one part of each evaluation while holding candidate responses and references fixed. Choose tasks for their measurement contribution. K3 adds hard coding problems after nearceiling pilots; Astra adds repository traces after inspecting upstream software tasks. Removing these groups, however, has only modest effects relative to same-domain, same-size random deletions. K3s addition improves Score but slightly reduces PA; Astras repository group leaves PA unchanged. By contrast, Astras spreadsheet tasks contribute strongly to both co-work metrics (Figure 4a,b). Task realism and difficulty motivate design, but its value depends on how it separates candidates in relation to the target. Many Astra spreadsheet responses exhaust their answer allowance, so the observed separation reflects the task under its chosen execution conditions. sections.title: 5 CASE STUDY: HOW RESEARCHERS REVISE EVALUATIONS
sections.content: Researchers use development feedback to expand coverage, repair tasks, and adjust execution. Astra develops repository-tracing tasks from source inspection, resolves promptrubric mismatches through pilot feedback, and adjusts execution after truncated responses. GLM corrects invalid examples and numerical answers, while K3 adds harder coding tasks after near-ceiling pilot scores. Section 4.3 analyzes these design choices; Appendix details the cases.

sections.title: 6 CONCLUSION
sections.content: ERB measures autonomous evaluation research under fixed budgets. Independent assessment separates score reproduction, ordering, and execution cost. Source inspection and pilot audits reveal how agents revise tasks and graders; component and subset analyses show why difficulty, nominal size, and measurement value must be assessed separately. This establishes an executable benchmark for the evaluation-design capability that autonomous improvement requires.

sections.title: D RESEARCH INSTRUCTIONS AND INPUTS
sections.content: Researchers are asked to design one executable evaluation with at least 100 distinct scored questions spanning coding, co-work, and reasoning. They may select, adapt, or synthesize tasks and choose graders, weights, grouping, and output allowances. During development, researchers compare directly measured candidate-domain scores with visible target-reference scores; final assessment reports Score and PA for frozen programs. The supplied workspace contains the task contract, development candidate APIs and available reference scores, original benchmark materials, available trajectories, and Python evaluation SDK. The SDK submits suite, records item-level responses and costs, and returns cross-model feedback on completed development tests. Researchers decide what to test, revise, and freeze within the threehour research period, $100 researcher wallet, and $100 shared development/helper wallet. Frozen assessment has separate $120 wallet and $30 per-candidate cap. The final program supplies executable questions, grading rules, and three fixed domain aggregations. Completed wrong or empty answers retain their grades; infrastructure failures remain incomplete. After freezing, the executor runs the candidate panel without sending assessment results back to the researcher. CASE STUDY: HOW RESEARCHERS REVISE EVALUATIONS The aggregate analyses show which design choices affect measurement, but do not explain how agents arrive at them. We now follow the saved research trajectories from source inspection through pilot testing and revision. Astra provides concrete example of this loop; GLM and K3 illustrate different responses to development feedback. Astra turns source inspection into coverage hypothesis. compact coding evaluation can miss repository-level behavior if it concentrates on isolated implementations. After inspecting upstream repository-investigation tasks, Astra identifies gap in its implementation-heavy coding bank and constructs eight multi-file repository traces. In one, candidates predict cached outputs and recomputation counts after in-place mutation versus replacing dependency object. Running the supplied fixture generates the expected outputs for grading (Figure 13a).

Astra examines these possibilities in performance-plan memo that scores 11/12: its response reports that 3/13 orders finish on time, but omits the mean close time required by the rubric. Astra finds that the question never explicitly requested that statistic and adds it to the brief. later audit also relaxes cloudmigration rubric that prescribed one architecture despite an open-ended brief, retaining the stated security and delivery requirements (Figure 13b,c). These revisions align prompts and graders before freezing; the saved pilot score precedes the repairs. Figure 13: Astras research loop. Source inspection motivates repository-tracing tasks; an 11/12 pilot exposes an implicit requirement, prompting clearer question; later validity audit broadens an overly restrictive rubric. The top strip shows saved versions (batch counts are not cumulative). The 112-question submission is then frozen for independent assessment. Researchers make different revisions from similar feedback. GLM corrects invalid examples and numerical answers; K3 responds to near-ceiling pilots with five hard coding tasks. Astra also changes answer allowances and grouped execution after truncated responses. These examples show three uses of pilot feedback: correcting task validity, extending coverage, and changing execution settings. The component analysis in Section 4.3 tests whether the resulting task groups improve agreement on the frozen candidate panel.
